title: Tendai
hook: the Japanese form of Tiantai on Mount Hiei, home of many founders

segments.voice: Yesterday, the golden lion: one gold, one shape, not two. Your line was gold and lion. What changed shape around you and kept its gold? A new week, and we cross the sea. Day one thousand three hundred thirty-eight.

Honen. Shinran. Eisai. Dogen. Nichiren. Say those names to someone who knows Japanese Buddhism and they'll hear founders: the Pure Land schools, Zen lines, the Nichiren schools. Teachers who went in different directions and sometimes argued hard. Now ask where each of them began. Tradition gives the same answer again and again: a forested mountain above Kyoto, where they studied as young monks before they ever founded anything. One slope, many roads leading down from it. The school on that slope is the Japanese form of the Tiantai we met this week: Tendai.
screen: `FOUNDERS IN MANY DIRECTIONS.` → `WHERE DID EACH BEGIN?` → `ONE SLOPE, MANY ROADS.`

segments.voice: First, the crossing. A Japanese monk named Saicho traveled to China, studied the Tiantai teaching, and brought it home to Mount Hiei. In Japanese the name is said Tendai. We met Saicho and his mountain earlier on this path. Today the question is a different one: what did the school hold, that so many roads could come out of it? Second, a rope of many strands. Tendai kept the Lotus Sutra at its center, as Tiantai did. But on Mount Hiei the monks also trained in meditation, kept the monastic precepts, practiced esoteric ritual with mantras and mandalas, and chanted the name of Amida Buddha. All under one roof. It was less a single practice than a whole curriculum. Third, the strands pulled out. Later teachers who trained there each, in his own way, took hold of one strand and found the whole rope in it. Honen and Shinran took the calling of Amida's name. Eisai and Dogen took meditation, and brought Zen lineages back from China. Nichiren took the Lotus Sutra itself. Their schools have their own stories, and the path will reach them soon. Fourth, why mother. Tradition calls Mount Hiei the mother mountain of Japanese Buddhism. A mother isn't the same as her children, and children don't always agree with their mother, or with each other. Some of these founders left the mountain in sharp disagreement. But the name holds something true: they learned to read, chant and sit in the same place. Tendai itself didn't vanish when its children left. It is still practiced on the mountain today, holding many strands at once.
screen: `SAICHO CARRIES TIANTAI HOME.` · `MANY STRANDS UNDER ONE ROOF.` · `EACH FOUNDER TAKES ONE STRAND.` · `A MOTHER, NOT A COPY.` · then, large: `THE MOTHER MOUNTAIN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: honor a mother-school. Sit, and let the breath settle. Then bring to mind a place that taught you before you went your own way. A school, a kitchen, a first job, a team, a congregation, a family. Maybe you left it gladly. Maybe you left it arguing. Either way, let one thing it gave you come up: a habit, a skill, a way of standing. Hold that for a few breaths. If you'd like, bow your head slightly toward it, inside. The bell holds the time.
Tendai. The Japanese form of Tiantai, founded on Mount Hiei by Saicho, holding the Lotus, meditation, precepts, ritual and the calling of Amida's name together. Today's word.
Your line: the mother mountain. Today, tell one person, or write one line, about a place that trained you, and what you still carry from it. Day one thousand three hundred thirty-eight.

howItsDone: Tendai Buddhists in Japan study the Lotus Sutra and combine meditation, precepts, esoteric ritual and recitation of Amida Buddha's name; Mount Hiei remains the school's center of training.
